title: Speaking and Listening: the spoken language endorsement
specPoints: Non-exam assessment: the Spoken Language endorsement, AO7 to AO9, reported separately as Pass, Merit or Distinction

tips.title: Separate grade, no marks, must be done
tips.body: Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified on the certificate; nothing towards the GCSE grade; assessed by the teacher against criteria that must all be met. The specification says each of these in plain words.

tips.title: The ladder's words
tips.body: Straightforward, challenging, sophisticated for ideas; an attempt, clear, a range of strategies for structure; straightforward, detailed, perceptive and elaborating for responses. Know which word the plan is reaching for.

tips.title: A topic without an argument stops at Pass
tips.body: My hobby gives information; why we should be allowed to run the library gives a position, reasons, an objection and an ask, and gives the questioner something to ask. Choose the second kind and agree it in advance.

tips.title: Three questions, three additions
tips.body: The money, the risk, the alternative: the obvious questions can be guessed. An elaboration kept back for each turns the hardest part of the assessment into the most prepared.

tips.title: Notes, not a script
tips.body: Reading a page is audible and intelligible and meets nobody's needs. Signposts and key sentences on a card, eyes on the room, and a pause at the turn.

tips.title: Answer the question asked
tips.body: AO8 begins with listening. Repeating the talk is not an answer; the question actually put, answered formally and in detail, then added to, is the Distinction response.

why.matters: Standing up in front of a room and holding it is the skill that interviews, meetings, lessons and every kind of leadership are made of, and the endorsement is the one place the qualification asks for it to be done rather than described. It carries no marks and it is on the certificate, which is the right way round: nobody is ever asked for their GCSE grade in a room they have to persuade, and everybody is judged on whether they can enrol the room, keep it, answer its questions and add something. The speech the writing topics taught is spoken here, and the questions afterwards are the part no exam paper can set.

examples.title: The interview
examples.body: A job interview is a presentation of five minutes and questions for twenty, and the criteria are the endorsement's: express the ideas, structure them for a listener, achieve the purpose, and answer the question actually asked with something more than was asked for. The student who has prepared three elaborations for a Year 10 talk has learned the thing interviewers are listening for.

examples.title: The meeting where something is decided
examples.body: A council chamber, a governors' meeting, a staff meeting, a family round a table: someone stands up, states what they want, gives reasons, meets the objection and asks for a specific thing, and then the questions come. The Distinction criteria are a description of the person in that room who gets what they asked for.

steps.title: What the endorsement is
steps.body:
Alongside the two written papers, every student gives a spoken presentation and is assessed on it by their teacher. The specification calls it the Spoken Language endorsement and sets three assessment objectives: AO7, demonstrate presentation skills in a formal setting; AO8, listen and respond appropriately to spoken language, including to questions and feedback; AO9, use spoken Standard English effectively in speeches and presentations.

**How it is reported.** As a separate grade, Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified, on the certificate. It carries no marks and does not contribute to the GCSE grade, and the specification says so in plain words. It must be done, and the school sends audio-visual recordings of a sample of students to AQA.

**How it is assessed.** Holistically, as a grade, on a competency basis: to be awarded a grade a student must meet all the criteria for that grade, and a student who does not reach Pass is recorded as Not Classified.

**What the school asks.** In Year 10, Summer 2: write and deliver a speech on a topic of the student's choice. The speech is the one the writing topics taught, spoken.

The talk itself: its content, structure, delivery
Listening and responding to questions and feedback
The questions afterwards, and any dialogue within the talk

check.prompt: How does the Spoken Language endorsement count towards the English Language GCSE grade?
check.solution: The specification says the endorsement will be reported as a separate grade and will not contribute to the result of the qualification. It has no marks; it is assessed holistically against criteria. It must still be completed.

options: It does not: it is reported separately as Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified, with no marks
It counts for ten per cent of the grade, the same weighting as AO1, and is added to the paper marks

steps.title: The criteria: Pass, Merit, Distinction
steps.body:
Every grade requires the general criteria: be audible; be intelligible; generally use language appropriate to the formal setting; use spoken Standard English. Then each grade adds its own, and all of them must be met.

**Pass.** Expresses straightforward ideas, information or feelings; makes an attempt to organise and structure the presentation; makes an attempt to meet the needs of the audience; listens to questions and feedback and responds appropriately in a straightforward manner.

**Merit.** Expresses challenging ideas, information or feelings using a range of vocabulary; organises and structures the presentation clearly and appropriately to meet the needs of the audience; achieves the purpose of the presentation; listens to questions and feedback, responding formally and in some detail.

**Distinction.** Expresses sophisticated ideas, information or feelings using a sophisticated repertoire of vocabulary; organises and structures the presentation using an effective range of strategies to engage the audience; achieves the purpose; listens to questions and feedback, responds perceptively and, if appropriate, elaborates with further ideas and information.

The ladder runs from straightforward to challenging to sophisticated; from an attempt at structure to clear structure to a range of strategies; from a straightforward response to a detailed one to a perceptive one that elaborates.

Challenging ideas, a range of vocabulary; clear structure; achieves the purpose

Sophisticated ideas and vocabulary; a range of strategies to engage; achieves the purpose

check.solution: The criteria run: appropriate and straightforward at Pass; formal and in some detail at Merit; perceptive, elaborating with further ideas, at Distinction. Answering a question by adding something the questioner had not thought of is the Distinction move.

steps.title: Choosing and agreeing the topic
steps.body:
The specification says students must identify the subject for their presentation in advance and agree it with their teacher, and that presentations must be planned and organised: lack of preparation is likely to prevent access to the criteria for the higher grades. The topic is the student's choice, and the choice decides how far the criteria can be reached.

**A topic with an argument in it.** Sophisticated ideas need something to be sophisticated about. *My hobby* gives information; *why the school should let us run the library* gives a position, reasons, an objection to meet and something to ask for, and the questions afterwards have somewhere to go.

**A topic you know more about than the room.** The Distinction criteria include elaborating with further ideas and information in answer to questions. That is only possible with a subject the speaker knows deeply.

**A topic that fits ten minutes.** The specification says no more than ten minutes as a guide. Five to seven minutes of talk and three of questions is usual, and a subject that needs twenty minutes will be cut in the wrong places.

**The forms allowed.** Talks, debates, speeches and dialogues, formal. Notes or slides may be used but are not required.

steps.title: Structure for the ear: a range of strategies
steps.body:
The Distinction criterion for structure is an effective range of strategies to engage the audience. The strategies are the ones the speech topic taught, plus the ones only a live room allows.

**An opening that enrols.** A question the room answers with its hands; a picture; a claim the room did not expect. Not *today I am going to talk about*.

**Signposting.** *Three reasons, and the third is the one I want you to remember.* A listener cannot look back.

**A shape.** Position, reasons, the objection met, an ending that asks: the five-line plan, spoken. The ending is the sentence the room repeats.

**Strategies the page cannot use.** The pause. The look up from the notes at the moment that matters. A change of pace at the turn. A question put to one person by name. A prop, or one slide with one picture on it. Each engages the room; each is a strategy the criteria name.

**Notes, not a script.** Reading aloud from a page is audible and intelligible and meets nobody's needs. Notes with the signposts and the key sentences, and eyes on the room.

check.prompt: Why does reading a script aloud limit the grade?
check.solution: The specification allows notes and slides, and a script is not forbidden; but the criteria from Merit up ask for structure that meets the audience's needs and strategies that engage them, and a face bent to a page shows neither. Notes with the signposts and eyes on the room.

visuals.problem: Plan a six-minute presentation arguing that the school should let students run the library at lunchtime.

steps.text: 0:00 to 0:30, the opening that enrols: hands up if you have been in the library at lunchtime this term; keep them up if it was open. Then the claim: it is shut three days in five, and we could open it.
steps.note: The room does something; the position arrives inside a fact.

steps.text: 0:30 to 1:00, the signpost: three reasons, and an objection I will answer, and then one thing I am asking for.
1:00 to 3:30, the reasons: the room is there and empty; the students who would run it have done harder jobs; the librarian has said she would train us. One case per reason, told in three sentences.
steps.note: Challenging ideas with a case each: Merit, reaching for Distinction.

steps.text: 3:30 to 4:30, the objection, met: it will be said that students cannot be trusted with the books. Here is the record of the last three years of lost books, and who lost them. A pause before the answer.
steps.note: The turn, with a change of pace and a pause: a strategy the room feels.

steps.text: 4:30 to 5:30, the ask: a trial for one half-term, two days a week, with a report to the head. Then the ending: the library has three hundred books nobody has read since 2019. Let us at least open the door.
steps.note: A specific ask; an ending the room repeats.

steps.text: 5:30 to 6:00, into questions: I have three minutes for questions, and I expect the first one to be about the money.

check.prompt: Why is the ask at the end specific, a trial for one half-term, two days a week?
check.solution: The criteria at Merit and Distinction include achieving the purpose. A talk that ends with a specific, answerable request has a purpose; one that ends with a hope does not. The room, and the teacher, can see whether the purpose was achieved.

steps.title: The questions: listening, then more
steps.body:
AO8 is listening and responding, and the criteria climb: appropriate and straightforward at Pass; formal and in some detail at Merit; perceptive, elaborating with further ideas and information, at Distinction. The questions are where a Merit becomes a Distinction, and they can be prepared for.

**Listen to the whole question.** Then answer the question asked, not the one expected. A response that repeats the talk is not listening.

**Answer formally, in Standard English, in some detail.** *Yes* is Pass. *Yes, and here is why, and here is the case that shows it* is Merit.

**Elaborate.** The Distinction word. Add something the questioner had not thought of: a further reason, a piece of information kept back for this, a consequence. Prepare three such additions for the three questions most likely to be asked.

**Respond to feedback as well as questions.** If the teacher or the room offers a view, take it seriously and answer it: agree with a difference, or disagree with a reason. That is responding perceptively.

**Ask a question back if it helps.** The specification includes asking questions to elicit clarification. *Do you mean the money for staffing, or the money for the books?* is listening made visible.

rows: Yes, I think it would work.
Yes, and the reason is the record of lost books, which shows that the students who use the library most lose the fewest.
Yes, and there is a further point I did not make: the school already trusts students with the equipment in the music rooms, which is worth more than the books. If that works, the library should.

check.prompt: What does elaborate mean in the Distinction criterion for responding to questions?
check.solution: The criterion is responds perceptively and, if appropriate, elaborates with further ideas and information. An answer that adds a reason or a consequence the room had not considered shows the speaker knows more than the talk contained, which is the Distinction mark of a well-chosen topic.

Speaking for longer than the question deserves, so that the assessor can hear more of the speaker's vocabulary

steps.title: Rehearse with a clock and a questioner
steps.body:
Plan a six-minute talk on a topic you know more about than the room, with an argument in it. Then rehearse it three times.

1. Once with a clock, to find the length. Cut from the middle, not the end.
2. Once to someone who will ask three questions, including the hardest one. Prepare an elaboration for each.
3. Once with the notes reduced to signposts and key sentences, eyes on the room.

Then check against the general criteria: audible from the back; intelligible; Standard English throughout; the register of a formal setting, which does not mean stiff.

check.prompt: A rehearsal runs to nine minutes when six were planned. Where should the cuts come from?
check.solution: The opening enrols the room and the ending is the sentence it repeats; both are strategies the criteria reward. The middle can lose a case without losing its shape. Dropping the questions would lose AO8 altogether.

markScheme.description: The middle: a reason shortened or a case cut, so the opening and the ending are kept

options: The ending, since the room will have stopped listening by then and the last minute is the one least often remembered
The opening, since it is only introduction and the room will not have settled in the first thirty seconds anyway
The middle: a reason shortened or a case cut, so the opening and the ending are kept
The questions, which can be dropped if the talk is long because they are not part of the presentation itself

steps.title: Distinction: sophisticated, engaging, perceptive
steps.body:
Distinction is not a mark out of anything; it is all of its criteria met. Four things to check the plan against.

**Sophisticated ideas with a sophisticated repertoire of vocabulary.** An argument with a turn in it, the kind the writing topics called complex, and the words for it chosen exactly rather than grandly.

**An effective range of strategies to engage the audience.** More than one: the opening that enrols, the signpost, the pause at the turn, the name, the ask. Range is the word.

**The purpose achieved.** A specific ask, made and answered.

**Perceptive responses that elaborate.** Three prepared additions, and the habit of answering the question actually asked.

**And the general criteria, without which nothing else counts:** audible, intelligible, Standard English, the register of a formal setting held even when the room laughs.

boxes.title: Perceptive, elaborating

check.prompt: A presentation is fluent, well organised and formal, and its speaker answers every question in some detail without adding anything. Which grade do the criteria give?
check.solution: The Merit criteria are met and the Distinction ones are not: responses that do not elaborate, and structure that is clear rather than a range of strategies, sit at Merit. The grade is holistic, and all the criteria for a grade must be met to reach it.

steps.title: The endorsement in one page
steps.body:
A presentation to a room, assessed by the teacher, reported as its own grade.

- **Three objectives:** AO7 presenting in a formal setting; AO8 listening and responding to questions and feedback; AO9 spoken Standard English.
- **Reported separately** as Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified; no marks; it does not count towards the GCSE grade, and it must be done.
- **The criteria climb:** straightforward, challenging, sophisticated ideas; an attempt at structure, clear structure, a range of strategies; straightforward, detailed, perceptive and elaborating responses. All the criteria for a grade must be met.
- **Choose a topic with an argument in it,** deeper than the room, that fits ten minutes, and agree it in advance.
- **Structure for the ear:** an opening that enrols, signposting, a turn with a pause, a specific ask; notes, not a script.
- **Prepare the questions:** three likely ones, three elaborations; answer the question asked.

The school sets it in Year 10 Summer 2 as a speech on a topic of the student's choice.

questions.solution:
Topic: the school should run a repair café one Saturday a term, staffed by students. 0:00 to 0:30, enrol: hands up if something in your house is broken and nobody knows how to fix it; keep them up if it is a phone. Claim: this building has the tools and the people to fix most of it. 0:30 to 1:00, signpost: three reasons, one objection, one ask. 1:00 to 2:00, reason one: the DT rooms are empty on Saturdays and the tools are already paid for. 2:00 to 3:00, reason two: eleven students in this year can solder, and two of them mended the science department's oscilloscope last term; case told in three sentences. 3:00 to 3:45, reason three: the town has a repair café that turns people away every month; the demand exists. 3:45 to 4:45, the objection, met, after a pause: it will be said that students cannot be insured to work on other people's property. The town café's insurance covers volunteers under sixteen with a supervising adult, and Mr Osei has offered to be that adult. 4:45 to 5:30, the ask: one Saturday in March, two hours, ten students, one teacher, and a report to the governors. Ending: there are things in this town that will go to landfill this year because nobody nearby could fix them. We could. Let us have one Saturday to prove it. 5:30 to 6:00, into questions.

Expected questions and elaborations. Who pays for parts? Elaboration: the town café asks for a donation and covers its parts that way; the average part costs less than a coffee, and most repairs need none. What if a student breaks something worse? Elaboration: every item is signed in with a form saying it is already broken and may not be fixable, which is what the town café does; I have a copy. Why should the school, rather than the town, do this? Elaboration: because the students learn something the town's volunteers already know, and because the governors have said they want more community projects; here is the line in the last governors' report.

criteria.text: The topic has a position, reasons, an objection and an ask, and the plan is timed to fit six minutes
The plan uses a range of strategies to engage the room: an opening that enrols, signposting, a pause or change of pace at the turn, a specific ask, an ending the room repeats
Three likely questions are named, each with a prepared elaboration that adds further ideas or information
The plan is written in Standard English and would be delivered from notes rather than read

questions.prompt: Write the first minute of your presentation as you would say it, about 150 words, so that it enrols the room, states the claim and signposts the shape. Then write the notes you would actually hold, reduced to signposts and key sentences, in no more than eight lines.
questions.solution:
Spoken. Hands up if there is something in your house that is broken and nobody knows how to fix. Keep them up if it is a phone. Right. Now look around, because this building has the tools to fix most of what is in your hands, and it has the people, and on Saturdays it has nothing else to do. I am going to ask for one Saturday. I have three reasons, and I know what the objection is going to be, so I will answer it before anyone has to ask. And at the end I am going to ask for something small enough that saying no would be embarrassing.

Notes. Hands up: broken; phone. Building has tools, people, Saturdays. ASK: one Saturday. Three reasons, one objection, one ask. R1 DT rooms empty, tools paid for. R2 eleven can solder; oscilloscope. R3 town café turns people away. OBJECTION insurance: town café covers under-16s; Mr Osei. ASK: March, two hours, ten students, one teacher, report to governors. END: landfill; we could; one Saturday.

questions.prompt: A presentation is given to the teacher alone. What does the specification require of it?
questions.solution: Where the audience is the teacher only, the presentation and dialogue must be designed so that they could have a potentially wider audience, the specification says, giving a television interview as an example.

markScheme.description: That it be designed so that it could have a wider audience than one person, like a television interview

options: That it be given twice, once to the teacher and once to a class, so that both a small and a large audience are met
Nothing different: an audience of one is the norm for the endorsement, and most presentations are given to the teacher alone
That it be designed so that it could have a wider audience than one person, like a television interview
That it be shortened to five minutes, since a single listener cannot be expected to attend for the full ten

questions.prompt: A student says: 'The endorsement doesn't count towards the grade, so it doesn't matter.' What is the better account?
questions.solution: The specification is clear that the endorsement does not contribute to the grade and equally clear that it is reported separately and must be done. Interviews, meetings, speeches and teaching all draw on it, and a Distinction is the first formal record of being able to hold a room.

markScheme.description: It is on the certificate as its own grade, it must be completed, and it is the one part of the qualification performed for a real room

options: The student is right, and the presentation can be given without preparation, since nothing that carries no marks can affect any result
It counts for twenty per cent of the grade, the same as AO6, so the student is mistaken about the marks and should prepare it like a paper
It only matters for students who want to study English at A level, since universities and sixth forms look at the endorsement grade
It is on the certificate as its own grade, it must be completed, and it is the one part of the qualification performed for a real room

examTechnique.body:
**No marks; a separate grade; all criteria met.** Pass, Merit or Distinction requires every criterion for that grade, on top of the general ones: audible, intelligible, Standard English, formal.

**Choose a topic with an argument in it,** deeper than the room, that fits ten minutes, and agree it with the teacher in advance. Lack of preparation shuts the higher grades.

**Structure for the ear:** enrol the room, signpost, reasons with a case each, the objection met with a pause, a specific ask, an ending the room repeats. A range of strategies is the Distinction word.

**Prepare the questions:** three likely ones, three elaborations. Listen to the whole question; answer it formally and in detail; add something.

**Notes, not a script.** Rehearse with a clock, a questioner and the notes alone.
examinerErrors: Reading a script, so that the eyes never leave the page and no strategy to engage the audience can be shown.
A topic with no argument in it, which gives information at Pass and leaves the questioner nothing to ask.
Answering questions by repeating the talk rather than listening to the question asked.
Slipping out of Standard English or out of the formal register when the room laughs or a question is hard.
Running long and cutting the ending, which is the part the room repeats.
Treating the endorsement as optional because it carries no marks, and giving an unprepared talk that is recorded as Not Classified.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: There is no grade 9 here; there is Distinction, and it looks like this: a topic with an argument in it that the speaker knows more deeply than the room, agreed in advance and planned to the minute; an opening that gives the room something to do, a signpost, reasons with a case each, an objection met after a pause, a specific ask and an ending the room repeats; sophisticated ideas in exact words, in Standard English, in a formal register that stays alive; and questions listened to, answered formally and in detail, and then added to with something the questioner had not thought of, three of them prepared in advance.
